title: Model eval and deploy options - Nova Insurance Discovery
summary: Initial model selection and deployment discovery for Nova Insurance. Focus on open-model comparison, context length needs (multi-tenant insurance docs, conversations), multilingual support (en/pt/es/fr), tool-calling for policy retrieval and claims automation, and security requirements for Private/VPC. Agreed next steps: run small-scale benchmark (cost & latency) on 8k vs 32k contexts, share security whitepaper and pricing ranges, schedule pilot kickoff for mid-September.
next_steps: Redwood to send security pack and SOC 2 report
Schedule 3-hour lab benchmark: 8k vs 32k with Nova sample prompts (target week of 2025-09-15)
Provide preliminary pricing ranges for hosted and Dedicated reserve
Follow-up call to review benchmark results and pilot plan (owner: Maya)
action_items: Maya Chen: send security pack + SOC2 + SAML integration notes (due 2025-09-04)
Diego Alvarez: prepare benchmark template and cost-latency spreadsheet (due 2025-09-10)
Arjun Patel (Nova): share redacted sample documents and conversational logs (due 2025-09-09)
Sofia Martins (Nova): provide compliance checklist and required audit dates (due 2025-09-05)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-02 16:00 UTC   Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Singh (Redwood SE backup), Priya Nair (Head of AI, Nova), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Sofia Martins (Compliance), Arjun Patel (Data Eng)

Auto-summary (may be imperfect): quick intro, discussion of model families (Mistral/Llama/Falcon/Gemma/Mixtral), context length needs for insurance docs and conversations, multilingual tokenization concerns, tool-calling for policy retrieval and claims system, hosted vs dedicated vs private pros/cons, security questions around KMS and audit logs.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, really appreciate you fitting this in. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya: Priya here, head of AI.
[00:10] Liam: Liam from platform.
[00:12] Sofia: Sofia, compliance.
[00:14] Arjun: Arjun, data eng.
[00:16] Diego: Diego from Redwood SE, hi all.
[00:18] Maya: Cool. Our goal today is to understand Nova's model selection criteria and deployment constraints so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private and propose a pilot. We expect the usual — trade-offs between latency/cost/quality and your security requirements.

[00:45] Priya: Right, high level — we have three main use cases: claim intake chat (conversational, multi-turn), automated policy summarization (long documents, attachments), and a backend extraction service for structured fields. Also we need multi-language support — English, Spanish, Portuguese, French — because of our LAC and EMEA customers.

[01:10] Maya: great, do you have an idea on the context window requirements for those? Like average and max token lengths?
[01:15] Arjun: For claim intake, average convo is 600-1200 tokens but we store history so end-to-end might hit 4k. Policy summarization — docs vary a lot, some policies + riders push 20k tokens, occasionally up to 28k.
[01:30] Liam: And with attachments (OCR'd PDF text) we could see the 30k-40k ballpark unless we chunk. We're trying to avoid losing context.

[01:50] Diego: ok so that already points to models with >32k context variants or approaches using chunking + retrieval. On the model side, are you prioritizing open-source models or are you open to proprietary?
[02:00] Priya: We'd prefer open-first because of cost and auditability, but if quality or tool-calling is significantly better on a closed model, we might consider it.

[02:20] Maya: noted. For open models there's a tradeoff: lighter models (e.g., Mixtral-ish families) are cheaper but may struggle on long-context summarization unless we use specialized 32k variants and indexing. Larger Llama-family or Mistral variants with 32k context exist; Falcon has strong throughput but historically weaker instruction-following on some tasks — though fine-tuning/rlhf or instruction tuning fixes a lot. Also Gemma has some enterprise optimizations — we can show empirical benchmarks.

[02:55] Priya: A question — tool-calling. We want the LLM to call our policy retrieval API and our claims system so it can fetch the right clause or policy holder record. How mature is Redwood's function/tool calling with open models?
[03:10] Diego: we've got several patterns: (1) built-in function-calling for models that natively support it (OpenAI-style), (2) shimmed approach where the Redwood runtime parses structured JSON from model output and routes to tooling, and (3) a deterministic extractor layer using small finetuned heads. For open models that don't have an official function-calling spec, we use client-side schema enforcement plus runtime validators. It's not magic but works reliably in production.
[03:45] Liam: What's the failure mode? If the model hallucinate params, do you have a validation layer?
[03:50] Diego: yes, we recommend a schema layer and short-circuit for any missing keys. Redwood's runtime has param validators and an optional sandbox for tool payloads. For high-sensitivity calls you can enforce allow-lists.

[04:15] Sofia: On compliance — data residency and audit logs are big for us. We need detailed request/response logs, encrypted at rest, keys managed via KMS/HSM, and SSO with SAML. Also SOC 2 and ISO roadmaps — do you have those?
[04:30] Maya: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II, ISO is in progress but we'll send the latest artifacts. For Private deployments we support bring-your-own-KMS and we can keep logs in your VPC. Hosted also supports customer-managed keys via KMS for payload encryption at rest. SSO/SAML is supported with RBAC. We'll share the security pack.

[05:02] Priya: Great. On latency — target for interactive chat is sub-200ms median for token streaming; for policy summarization batch jobs we can tolerate higher latency. Do your open models hit that?
[05:18] Diego: Depends on model size and infra. Smaller quantized weights on Dedicated hardware can get to sub-200ms for small sequences, but for 32k context runs latency is higher. We optimize with KV-cache, continuous batching, and compiled kernels. For hosted customers we publish performance profiles per model; for Dedicated you can reserve GPUs tuned to your needs.

[05:45] Arjun: Is quantization supported for the long-context variants? We worry about quality regressions.
[05:50] Ravi: yes, quantization generally helps cost but can introduce subtle hallucination issues; we provide recommended quant profiles tied to eval sets so you can see quality delta. For Nova we'd recommend running evals on your policy summarization prompts to pick a safe quant profile.

[06:20] Priya: Let's talk about multilingual quality. Spanish and Portuguese are high priority; French secondary. Are certain model families better?
[06:28] Diego: In our benchmarks, Llama-extended and Mistral-variants tend to be balanced across languages; some regionally trained models are stronger in specific languages. We often ensemble: use a smaller local model for cheap translation/normalization and a larger model for semantic tasks. Tokenization can blow up costs for some languages — we should test with your text.

[06:55] Liam: We also need to integrate with our internal vector DB for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Does Redwood integrate with common vector stores?
[07:02] Maya: yes — we have connectors for Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, and vector DBs behind your VPC. Retrieval can be performed in your VPC for private pilot. We can also run hybrid rerank on the Redwood side if you prefer.

[07:25] Priya: On pilot scope — what's realistic? We want a pilot that proves both cost and fidelity for policy summarization and the claim intake flow.
[07:33] Maya: typical pilot: (1) we provision a dedicated test pool or hosted test tenant, (2) we run a set of 100-200 prompts across your sample documents and convo logs, measuring latency/cost/ROUGE/semantic-similarity and hallucination rate, (3) we iterate on model & quant settings and instrument the tool-calling validator. We can do that in 2-3 weeks.

[08:00] Sofia: Will logs from the pilot be stored in your systems? We need to redaction and retention policies.
[08:07] Maya: we can either host logs encrypted with your KMS, or store logs in your VPC. We support automated PII redaction hooks and retention windows. We'll include the policy in the security pack.

[08:30] Priya: Cost — rough ballpark between hosted and dedicated? We need ranges to justify to finance.
[08:35] Maya: for open models, hosted pay-as-you-go has higher per-token but no infra upfront; Dedicated with reserved capacity cuts per-token by a factor depending on volume — typically 30-60% saving at steady-state. Exact numbers depend on model and quantization. We'll send a model-cost calculator.

[09:05] Liam: Are there specific models Redwood recommends for long-context summarization?
[09:10] Diego: We usually recommend exploring (a) a 32k-capable Llama/Mistral variant for one-pass summarization, (b) RAG with a 8k base model for chunked retrieval if docs >32k, or (c) a mixture: use a 32k context for key parts and retrieval for deep history. We also suggested running both 8k and 32k tests to compare cost/quality — you'll see tradeoffs.

[09:45] Priya: About model governance — we want model versioning and rollout controls, plus ability to pin specific versions per route. Does Redwood support that?
[09:52] Maya: yes — pinned versions, canary rollouts, A/B tests, automatic fallback. Console exposes token-level cost and latency and route-level dashboards.

[10:10] Arjun: Any red flags we should be aware of in private/on-prem setup?
[10:14] Diego: network egress and GPU procurement timelines are typical blockers; on-prem can take months. VPC-deployed private control plane is faster — usually a few weeks. Also licensing for some model weights varies; open models are simpler but check the license for weights you pick.

[10:40] Priya: We also have a procurement timeline — CFO review in 6 weeks, and security approval in 4 weeks. So we need materials fast.

[10:50] Maya: understood — we'll prioritize the security pack and pricing ranges. Also we'll propose a bench schedule matching your procurement dates so results are available before CFO review.

[11:10] Sofia: Quick nit — our compliance team will want to know about immutable audit trails and whether log tampering is possible.
[11:18] Ravi: logs are write-once within the KMS-backed store and we can provide audit digests. For private deployments you control the storage. We'll document the capabilities.

[11:35] Liam: A couple technical clarifications — how do you handle KV cache eviction with multi-tenant workloads? If we have a hot policy reference that's used a lot, will it stay cached?
[11:44] Diego: Redwood's runtime is workload-aware: it keeps prefix/KV caches for active sessions and offers configurable TTLs and pinning for hot keys. For dedicated pools you can reserve more cache capacity.

[12:05] Priya: On hallucination tracking — do you provide automated QA or metric computation?
[12:12] Maya: yes, Redwood Optimize can run eval suites comparing outputs to golden summaries and surface regressions. We can tie alerts to new model releases. For the pilot we'll include a small eval harness.

[12:35] Arjun: We'll want to test function-calling to our internal claims API. Some endpoints require MFA token exchange — is there a recommended pattern?
[12:45] Diego: we recommend short-lived service tokens minted by your auth flow; Redwood can support token exchange via a secure webhook. For high-security endpoints, we recommend an allow-list and parameter scrubbing.

[13:10] Priya: Any thoughts on fallback policies if a model is down in a region?
[13:15] Maya: you can configure smart routing by latency or cost; automatic fallback to a smaller compatible model in another region; and automatic retries with degraded QoS. For insurance-critical paths you might run synchronous verification calls or degrade to read-only retrieval.

[13:45] Liam: Do you have any partnerships for cloud marketplace procurement?
[13:50] Maya: yes we integrate with AWS Marketplace and GCP — can do meter billing through marketplace if that helps procurement.

[14:10] Priya: OK, let's recap next steps.
[14:13] Maya: recap: Redwood sends security pack + SOC2 + SAML guide (Maya), benchmark template and cost calc (Diego), we schedule 3-hour bench week of 2025-09-15, Nova shares redacted sample docs and conv logs (Arjun), Nova compliance sends checklist (Sofia). Any other items?
[14:35] Sofia: also send the log retention and redaction details.
[14:38] Maya: will do.

[14:50] Priya: Sounds good. We're excited to see how this performs.
[14:54] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up by end of Thursday with the artifacts.
[15:00] Diego: thanks everyone.

Notes on transcript quality: some brand names and acronyms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache as KV cash, VPC as V P C), timestamps approximate.

Shared artifacts referenced: security-pack.pdf (link sent post-call), benchmark-template.xlsx (to be shared), costing-calculator.csv (to be shared).

End of transcript.
